items.title: How Rust Changed Me As A Developer
items.summary: performance, rust
items.content:
The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer

1 . That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript

pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or

develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a

programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you.

Rust was quite different to me, so it did.

I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years

now . One of the reasons I really wanted to

become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and

hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.

What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can

encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered

quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into

We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:

The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each

other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first

names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to

But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that

the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3 : the sum

type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another,

Human { first_name: String , last_name: String },

Cat { name: String , cuteness: Cuteness }

A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities.

Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type,

but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where

you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on

the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.

// do a thing with first_name and last_name

When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and

last_name . You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These

It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People

using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model

optionality ( null ) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can

also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of

success), or an error (with a value describing the error).

Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can

simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to

help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.

In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic

dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:

The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the

details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.

This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may

not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the

Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an

interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using

humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely

worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you

need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses

them -- you want your code use the open/closed

But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to

be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in

other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.

Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to

add Dog . Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

items.title: Cyber Attack Hits 178 Major Websites including IKEA, SaleForce, GitLab, Zoom by using Optimizely.
items.content:
See more of our trusted coverage when you search. Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search.

Hackers have planted malicious code on some of the world's most popular websites, potentially exposing visitors to the theft of their personal and financial information, cybersecurity experts have warned.

Security researcher Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, told Newsweek in an email Tuesday that researchers found at least 188 infected Optimizely projects across 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Salesforce and Equifax.

Helme estimated that the malicious code may have been served during roughly 34 million page visits, with a broad possible range of 6 million to 150 million. He added: “That counts visits that loaded the code, not people who lost money or data. The actual harm is far smaller.”

According to Helme, the code could steal payment-card details, swap cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture cookies and screenshots and redirect older iPhones and iPads to an exploit kit. Researchers could see about $7,000 in cryptocurrency reach wallets linked to the attacker, he said, although they could not determine how many card numbers may have been stolen.

“This is a supply-chain attack: Compromise one trusted vendor, and its code runs on every customer's website at once,” Helme said, adding that researchers had seen “no evidence of AI involvement.”

The attack may have affected websites including Zoom, CNN, HSBC, the BBC, IKEA, Salesforce, Equifax, Fox News, Alaska Airlines and GitLab, according to researchers at cybersecurity firm Report URI who identified the attack on Monday. A full list is provided below.

Hackers injected malicious JavaScript, a common computer language, into scripts hosted by Optimizely, a company that provides software allowing businesses to test different versions of websites, the researchers said.

Optimizely said in a status update on its website on Tuesday that "an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability" in its Experimentation platform. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects," it said.

"The most important take-away is not that malicious code appeared on websites associated with 178 major organizations. It is that a vulnerability in one shared technology provider can potentially expose people across otherwise unrelated businesses and industries to consequences they never expected or were prepared for," John Walsh, Field CTO at IGEL told Newsweek in an email Tuesday.

The 6 Stages of FaceStealer: Are You a Victim of North Korean Scam?

Walsh said the "potential exposure could extend into the millions and [tens] of millions given the combined reach of the organizations identified. But we must distinguish potential exposure, execution of malicious code, and confirmed compromise."

"The 178 organizations represent potentially affected websites, not 178 confirmed corporate breaches or a known number of victims," he said. "A defensible victim estimate requires traffic during the exposure window, the specific pages and scripts involved, and forensic evidence of successful theft."

Peter Lowe, threat research lead at ZeroFox, explained the attack as "a third-party supply chain attack."

"The sites affected weren’t breached in the usual sense at all—their own code and infrastructure were fine, they were loading JavaScript from a provider they trusted, and that trust is what got exploited," Lowe told Newsweek on Tuesday. " There's been a lot of discussion lately about offensive AI frameworks and I wouldn't be surprised to find out that this is an example attack."

Consumer credit reporting company Equifax told Newsweek that it was aware of the reports and had "immediately investigated this issue and ceased our use of Optimizely."

"We have not identified evidence of any compromise to our systems or impact to our data," it added.

items.title: Nimony: The next version of Nim
items.summary: compilers, programming
items.content:
Built every day from nimony’s master branch.

Unpack, put bin/ on your PATH , done — and with

nimony n you do not even need a C compiler.

Nimony is a new compiler for Nim and the home of the Nim 3 language: borrow checking, explicit nilability, sum types, checked generics and more, with incremental and parallel builds from the start. For how it relates to Nim 2, see the FAQ .

Variant objects no longer need a separate discriminator enum: tags live in the case section, and `case value of Tag(fields):` pattern matching binds the fields for that arm — like expressions you’d write in ML-family languages, checked for exhaustiveness.

echo eval ( Add ( left : Lit ( value : 10 ) , right : Lit ( value : 32 ) ) ) # 42

Shared fields can live outside the case , variants can nest ( seq[Tree] in a branch), and grouped matchers like {Add, Sub}(left, right) appear where multiple tags share the same shape — see Case in object in the manual .

Nimony rejects classic footguns at compile time:

proc grow ( s : var seq [ int ] ; use : int ) =

# grow(s, v) # Error: `s` is borrowed during iteration — no realloc under active borrows

This follows prefix exclusion : while s (or s.elements ) is borrowed, that path cannot be mutated until the borrow ends — sibling fields can still be updated.

By default generics are type checked: the code is checked when the generic is defined , not only when it is instantiated! Duck typing is still available, you get it via the {.untyped.} pragma.

The required operations are described via concepts:

proc min [ T : Comparable ] ( a , b : T ) : T =

Container-style concepts (e.g. Findable[T] ) work the same way with iterators and indexed access — see Concepts and Generics in the manual .

2026-09-08 Nimony 0.6.2 has been released. It ships with a guest report from a user who spent a year porting real projects over. A Vulkan visualiser, a web framework, an embedded server: Nim, one year in .

Older entries, including the 0.2 release , live on the News page.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.
